title: Visual Analysis
text: This report investigates the profitability (loss ratio = total incurred / total premium) and volatility (variability of the loss ratio) of a Spanish motor insurance portfolio containing 354,140 policy-year records across 2022 to 2024. The analysis proceeds in four stages: data wrangling, univariate exploration of key variables, bivariate analysis to identify drivers of loss ratio, and interactive visualisations for deeper exploration.

  show_col_types = FALSE
)

1.2 Select Relevant Columns
The 47 columns include coverage-level breakdowns of premium, claims and incurred amounts (e.g. liability_premium, theft_claims, fire_incurred). These are sub-components of the three totals — total_premium, total_claims and total_incurred — which are already retained. Since the objective is portfolio-level profitability and volatility, the breakdowns add no analytical value. select() retains only the 19 columns needed.

policy <- policy_raw %>%
  select(
    insured_id, year,
    policy_type, policy_status, business_type,
    payment_frequency, bonus_score,
    driver_age, vehicle_age, age_driving_licence,
    fuel_type, vehicle_value, vehicle_brand,
    municipality_type, circulation_area,
    total_premium, total_incurred,
    total_claims, total_exposure
  )

cat("Columns kept:   ", ncol(policy), "\n")

The dataset is reduced from 47 to 19 columns. The 28 removed columns are all coverage-level breakdowns (liability, property, theft, fire, glass, legal protection, occupants) for premium, claims and incurred amounts.

title: Visual Analysis
section: 1.4 Cast Factors and Derive New Variables
text:
1.4 Cast Factors and Derive New Variables
Two transformations are applied:
Factors — eight categorical columns are cast to ordered factors with readable labels. This controls axis ordering in plots and replaces raw codes (e.g. “A”, “G”) with meaningful labels (e.g. “Active”, “Good”). vehicle_brand is simplified to the top 10 brands with all others collapsed to “Other”.
Derived variables — seven new columns are computed. These are the core metrics used in every subsequent visual analysis.

policy <- policy %>%
  mutate(
    year = as.integer(year),

    policy_type = factor(policy_type,
                         levels = c("TP","TPG","CC","COMP_E","COMP_N")),

    policy_status = factor(policy_status,
                           levels = c("A","C"),
                           labels = c("Active","Cancelled")),

    business_type = factor(business_type,
                           levels = c("NB","P"),
                           labels = c("New Business","Portfolio")),

    payment_frequency = factor(payment_frequency,
                               levels = c("A","S","Q"),
                               labels = c("Annual","Semi-annual","Quarterly")),

    bonus_score = factor(bonus_score,
                         levels = c("G","N","B"),
                         labels = c("Good","Neutral","Bad")),

    fuel_type = factor(fuel_type,
                       levels = c("D","G"),
                       labels = c("Diesel","Gasoline")),

    municipality_type = factor(municipality_type,
                               levels = c("I","C","IS"),
                               labels = c("Inland","Coastal","Islands")),

    circulation_area = factor(circulation_area,
                              levels = c("U","R"),
                              labels = c("Urban","Rural")),

    vehicle_brand = if_else(
      vehicle_brand %in% (count(., vehicle_brand, sort = TRUE) %>%
                          slice_head(n = 10) %>% pull(vehicle_brand)),
      vehicle_brand, "Other"),
    vehicle_brand = factor(vehicle_brand),

    loss_ratio      = total_incurred / total_premium,
    claim_frequency = total_claims   / total_exposure,
    severity        = total_incurred / total_claims,
    has_claim       = total_claims   > 0,

    loss_ratio_bins = cut(loss_ratio,
                          breaks = c(-Inf, 0, 0.5, 1, Inf),
                          labels = c("Zero","0-0.5","0.5-1","Above 1")),

    driver_age_band = cut(driver_age,
                          breaks = c(17,25,35,45,55,65,Inf),
                          labels = c("18-25","26-35","36-45",
                                     "46-55","56-65","65+")),

    vehicle_age_band = cut(vehicle_age,
                           breaks = c(-1,5,10,15,20,Inf),
                           labels = c("0-5","6-10","11-15",
                                      "16-20","20+"))
  )

title: Visual Analysis
text:
2.1 Portfolio Composition — Categorical Variables
geom_bar() with geom_text(stat = "count") displays both count and percentage directly on each bar. coord_flip() improves label readability. patchwork combines four charts using | and / operators.

Portfolio CompositionBonus Score




Code
bar_label <- function(df, var, title) {
  ggplot(df, aes(x = fct_rev({{ var }}))) +
    geom_bar(fill = "#6BAED6") +
    geom_text(
      stat = "count",
      aes(label = paste0(after_stat(count), ",  ",
                         round(after_stat(count) /
                               sum(after_stat(count)) * 100, 1), "%")),
      hjust = -0.1, size = 2.8
    ) +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.3))) +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme(axis.text.x  = element_blank(),
          axis.ticks.x = element_blank())
}

p1 <- bar_label(policy, policy_type,       "Policy Type")
p2 <- bar_label(policy, payment_frequency,  "Payment Frequency")
p3 <- bar_label(policy, municipality_type,  "Municipality Type")
p4 <- bar_label(policy %>% filter(!is.na(fuel_type)), fuel_type, "Fuel Type")

(p1 | p2) / (p3 | p4) +
  plot_annotation(
    title      = "Composition of the Motor Insurance Portfolio",
    subtitle   = "Count and percentage of policies across four key categorical variables",
    tag_levels = "A",
    theme = theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#f5f5f5",
                                                 colour = "#f5f5f5"))
  )









Observations
CC policy type dominates at 57.8% of all policies. Annual payment accounts for over 80%. Inland is the largest geographic segment and Diesel is the dominant fuel type. TP (5,757 policies) and Islands (24,140 policies) are relatively small segments — statistical results for these groups should be treated cautiously.




Code
ggplot(policy, aes(x = fct_rev(bonus_score))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#6BAED6") +
  geom_text(stat = "count",
            aes(label = paste0(after_stat(count), ",  ",
                               round(after_stat(count) /
                                     sum(after_stat(count)) * 100, 1), "%")),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 2.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.25))) +
  labs(title = "Bonus Score Distribution",
       subtitle = "Good = clean history, Neutral = average, Bad = frequent claimant",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank())









Observations
96.4% of policies are rated Good. Neutral and Bad together account for only 245 policies. Bonus score has limited segmentation power and statistical tests comparing Good vs Bad should be interpreted cautiously due to the extreme imbalance.

title: Visual Analysis
text:
2.2 Key Numerical Variables — Distribution
A histogram stacked beneath a boxplot is used. The boxplot reveals outliers and skewness while the histogram shows the full shape. Mean (pink) and median (purple) are annotated. A reusable hist_box() function avoids code repetition.

hist_box <- function(df, var, var_label) {
  v     <- df %>% filter(!is.na({{ var }})) %>% pull({{ var }})
  m_mn  <- round(mean(v), 1)
  m_med <- round(median(v), 1)

  hist_p <- ggplot(df %>% filter(!is.na({{ var }})),
                   aes(x = {{ var }})) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = "#6BAED6", colour = "#f5f5f5") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = m_med, colour = "#595DE5",
               linewidth = 0.7, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = m_mn, colour = "#e0218a",
               linewidth = 0.7, linetype = "dashed") +
    annotate("text", x = m_med, y = Inf,
             label = paste0("Median = ", m_med),
             colour = "#595DE5", hjust = -0.1, vjust = 1.5, size = 3) +
    annotate("text", x = m_mn, y = Inf,
             label = paste0("Mean = ", m_mn),
             colour = "#e0218a", hjust = -0.1, vjust = 3.2, size = 3) +
    labs(x = var_label, y = NULL) +
    theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())

  box_p <- ggplot(df %>% filter(!is.na({{ var }})),
                  aes(y = {{ var }}, x = "")) +
    geom_boxplot(fill = "#6BAED6",
                 outlier.colour = "#d18a7d",
                 outlier.shape  = 16,
                 outlier.size   = 0.8) +
    stat_summary(geom = "point", fun = "mean",
                 colour = "#e0218a", size = 3) +
    stat_boxplot(geom = "errorbar", width = 0.5) +
    coord_flip() +
    theme(axis.text  = element_blank(),
          axis.ticks = element_blank())

  (box_p / hist_p) + plot_layout(heights = c(1, 3.5))
}


Driver AgeVehicle AgeTotal PremiumVehicle ValueTotal IncurredTotal ClaimsClaim Frequency




Code
hist_box(policy, driver_age, "Driver Age (years)")









Observations
The portfolio is dominated by middle-aged drivers between 40 and 60 years old with a median age of 48. Young drivers under 25 are very few — the insurer appears to either price them out or actively avoid this high-risk group. A small number of elderly drivers in their 80s appear as outliers on the right but are too few to affect the overall picture.




Code
hist_box(policy, vehicle_age, "Vehicle Age (years)")









Observations
The typical vehicle is 25 years old — remarkably old by European standards. This is not a new-car portfolio. The distribution shows two clusters, suggesting two types of customers: those with moderately old cars (15 to 20 years) and those keeping very old vehicles on the road (30 to 35 years). Vehicles older than 40 years appear as outliers. Older vehicles tend to have more mechanical failures, creating unpredictable claims costs.




Code
hist_box(policy, total_premium, "Total Premium (EUR)")









Observations
Most policies pay between EUR 100 and EUR 600 in annual premium with a median of EUR 258. The histogram shows two visible clusters — a large group of low-premium policies and a smaller group of higher-premium policies. The long right tail with outliers extending beyond EUR 3,000 is visible in the boxplot, while the mean (EUR 297) sits only slightly above the median confirming extreme values are rare.




Code
hist_box(policy %>% filter(!is.na(vehicle_value)),
         vehicle_value, "Vehicle Value (EUR)")









Observations
Most vehicles are valued around EUR 25,000 but a small number of luxury or classic cars are worth up to EUR 400,000 — visible as isolated dots far to the right of the boxplot. Despite these extreme outliers, the mean and median are close together confirming the extreme values are very rare. These high-value vehicles are the biggest individual risk in the portfolio — a single claim could generate a loss ratio many times larger than the premium collected.




Code
hist_box(policy %>% filter(total_incurred > 0),
         total_incurred, "Total Incurred (EUR) — Policies With Claims Only")









Observations
Total incurred is extremely right-skewed even after excluding zero-claim policies. The median incurred amount is modest but the boxplot reveals extreme outliers representing very large individual claims. These extreme claims are the primary driver of portfolio volatility.




Code
hist_box(policy %>% filter(total_claims > 0),
         total_claims, "Total Claims — Policies With At Least One Claim")









Observations
Among policies that made at least one claim, the vast majority made exactly one claim. Two or more claims per policy are rare. This confirms that most loss-making events are single-incident rather than repeat claiming behaviour.




Code
hist_box(policy %>% filter(is.finite(claim_frequency),
                           claim_frequency > 0,
                           claim_frequency < 3),
         claim_frequency, "Claim Frequency (claims per year) — Claimants Only")









Observations
Among policies with at least one claim, the median claim frequency is exactly 1.0 — the typical claimant makes precisely one claim per policy-year. The mean of 1.4 is pulled above the median by a small number of policies making multiple claims, visible as the secondary spike at exactly 2.0. The two distinct spikes at 1.0 and 2.0 reflect the integer nature of claim counts.

title: Visual Analysis
section: 2.3 Vehicle Age by Fuel Type — Grouped Density
text:
2.3 Vehicle Age by Fuel Type — Grouped Density
geom_density() overlays two smoothed distributions on the same axis, enabling direct shape comparison between Diesel and Gasoline vehicles.

ggplot(policy %>% filter(!is.na(fuel_type)),
       aes(x = vehicle_age, colour = fuel_type, fill = fuel_type)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Diesel" = "#2171B5", "Gasoline" = "#e0218a")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values  = c("Diesel" = "#2171B5", "Gasoline" = "#e0218a")) +
  labs(title = "Gasoline Vehicles Show a Bimodal Age Distribution",
       subtitle = "Kernel density estimate overlaying two groups on the same axis",
       x = "Vehicle Age (years)", y = "Density",
       colour = "Fuel Type", fill = "Fuel Type")








Observations
Diesel vehicles have a sharp peak at around 18 years, meaning Diesel owners are concentrated in the 10 to 25 year vehicle age range. Gasoline vehicles show a clear bimodal distribution with two peaks with one at around 25 years and a second at around 35 years, suggesting two distinct customer segments. The two curves overlap closely between 20 and 30 years but diverge significantly beyond 30 where Gasoline has considerably more mass, meaning Gasoline vehicles are more likely to be very old and may generate higher maintenance-related claims.

title: Visual Analysis
section: 2.4 Vehicle Value by Policy Type — Violin Plot
text:
2.4 Vehicle Value by Policy Type — Violin Plot
A violin plot shows the full density shape per group. An inner boxplot is overlaid with geom_boxplot(width = 0.1) to retain median and IQR information. Mean is added via stat_summary().

ggplot(policy %>% filter(!is.na(vehicle_value)),
       aes(x = policy_type, y = vehicle_value)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "#6BAED6", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, fill = "white", outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_summary(geom = "point", fun = "mean",
               colour = "#e0218a", size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Comprehensive Policies Cover Higher-Value Vehicles",
       subtitle = "Violin plot with inner boxplot and mean point (pink)",
       x = "Policy Type", y = "Vehicle Value (EUR)")








Observations
All five policy types have most vehicle values clustered near zero, reflected in the flat and wide violin bases. COMP_E and COMP_N stand out with higher mean points and slightly less flat bases, indicating their vehicles are more spread across a wider value range. CC has the longest upper tail reaching EUR 350,000 due to its large policy count rather than genuinely higher vehicle values. The overall pattern confirms that comprehensive policyholders tend to own more expensive vehicles, which directly drives higher claim costs when damage occurs.

title: Visual Analysis
section: 2.5 Loss Ratio Distribution — The Headline Metric
text:
2.5 Loss Ratio Distribution — The Headline Metric
Because 88% of policies have zero incurred losses, the chart is restricted to policies where both total_claims > 0 and total_incurred > 0. The excluded proportion is calculated dynamically and annotated on the chart.

pct_excluded <- scales::percent(
  1 - mean(policy$total_claims > 0 & policy$total_incurred > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
  accuracy = 0.1)

claims_only <- policy %>%
  filter(total_claims > 0, total_incurred > 0,
         is.finite(loss_ratio), loss_ratio < 5)

max_y <- claims_only %>%
  pull(loss_ratio) %>%
  cut(breaks = seq(0, 5, length.out = 41)) %>%
  table() %>% max()

ggplot(claims_only, aes(x = loss_ratio)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#6BAED6", colour = "#f5f5f5") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "firebrick",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.08, y = max_y * 0.6,
           label = "Break-even\n(LR = 1)",
           colour = "firebrick", hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 3, y = max_y * 0.9,
           label = paste0(pct_excluded, " of policies\nexcluded\n(no paid claims)"),
           colour = "#2171B5", hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  labs(title = "Among Policies With Paid Claims, Many Exceed Break-Even",
       subtitle = paste0("Showing ", scales::comma(nrow(claims_only)),
                         " policies with at least one paid claim (",
                         pct_excluded, " excluded)"),
       x = "Loss Ratio  (incurred / premium)",
       y = "Number of Policies With a Claim")








Observations
Of the 32,637 policies with at least one paid claim, more sit below break-even than above it — meaning the majority of claimants are still profitable for the insurer. However the distribution does not drop sharply after LR = 1. Instead it declines gradually and remains substantial all the way to LR = 5, meaning loss-making claims are not rare outliers but a persistent and sizable tail. The portfolio profits from the 88.1% who never claim, but remains exposed to a long tail of severe claimants that is difficult to price away.

title: Visual Analysis
section: 3.1 Policy Type — The Primary Driver of Loss Ratio
text:
3.1 Policy Type — The Primary Driver of Loss Ratio
Policy type is examined first as it is the most actionable pricing variable. Three complementary charts are used: a boxplot for the distribution shape, a statistical test for significance, and a claim rate chart to decompose the mechanism.

Boxplot — Loss Ratio by Policy TypeStatistical Test — Kruskal-WallisClaim Rate by Policy Type




Code
policy %>%
  filter(is.finite(loss_ratio), loss_ratio < 5) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = policy_type, y = loss_ratio)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#6BAED6",
               outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_summary(geom = "point", fun = "mean",
               colour = "#e0218a", size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "firebrick",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = 1.05,
           label = "Break-even", colour = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 2)) +
  labs(title = "COMP_N Has the Highest Mean Loss Ratio Across All Policy Types",
       subtitle = "Boxplot zoomed to 0-2. Pink point = mean. Dashed = break-even.",
       x = "Policy Type", y = "Loss Ratio (zoomed to 0-2)")









Observations
All five policy types have medians near zero and means well below break-even, meaning every segment is profitable on average. A clear gradient emerges as TP and TPG means sit closest to zero while COMP_N’s mean at approximately 0.5 is the highest of all types. COMP_N is also the only segment with a visible IQR box, indicating meaningfully more spread in its loss ratios. While COMP_N remains profitable on average, its wider distribution and higher mean signal that it carries the most risk.




Code
ggbetweenstats(
  data     = policy %>% filter(is.finite(loss_ratio), loss_ratio < 5),
  x        = policy_type,
  y        = loss_ratio,
  type     = "np",
  pairwise.comparisons = TRUE,
  pairwise.display     = "s",
  p.adjust.method      = "fdr",
  messages  = FALSE,
  title     = "Kruskal-Wallis Test — Loss Ratio Differs Significantly Across Policy Types",
  xlab      = "Policy Type",
  ylab      = "Loss Ratio"
)









Observations
All five policy types have a median loss ratio of exactly 0.00, meaning more than half of policies in every segment make no claims at all. COMP_N is the only type with a visible interquartile range box, confirming it has the most spread. The Kruskal-Wallis test confirms overall differences are statistically significant (p = 2.23e-308), and all pairwise FDR-corrected comparisons show significant p-values. Hence we can say that every policy type is genuinely different from every other. Despite identical medians, COMP_N carries far more variability in loss outcomes.




Code
policy %>%
  group_by(policy_type) %>%
  summarise(claim_rate = mean(has_claim) * 100, n = n()) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = policy_type, y = claim_rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#6BAED6", width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(claim_rate, 1), "%",
                               "\n(n=", scales::comma(n), ")")),
            vjust = -0.3, size = 3.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 50), labels = NULL) +
  labs(title = "COMP_N Policies Claim Most Frequently — Over 3x the TP Rate",
       subtitle = "Percentage of policies with at least one claim by policy type",
       x = "Policy Type", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.ticks.y = element_blank())









Observations
Claim rate rises steadily as cover becomes more comprehensive. TP has the lowest claim rate at 6.9% meaning that customers with basic third-party only cover tend to absorb small damages themselves rather than claim. COMP_N has the highest at 31.3%. The jump from COMP_E (18.5%) to COMP_N (31.3%) is particularly striking given that these two products offer the same breadth of cover. The only difference is the excess. This single design feature nearly doubles the claim rate, directly explaining why COMP_N generates higher loss ratios than COMP_E.

title: Visual Analysis
section: 3.2 Loss Distribution by Policy Type and Bonus Score — Ridgeline Plots
text:
3.2 Loss Distribution by Policy Type and Bonus Score — Ridgeline Plots
stat_density_ridges() with ECDF gradient and quantile lines reveals how loss ratio distributions differ in shape across segments, beyond what boxplots can show.

By Policy Type (ECDF fill)By Bonus Score (Quantile lines)




Code
policy %>%
  filter(is.finite(loss_ratio),
         loss_ratio < 5) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = loss_ratio,
             y = fct_rev(policy_type),
             fill = 0.5 - abs(0.5 - after_stat(ecdf)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom      = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE,
    alpha     = 0.8,
    scale     = 1.5
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Probability", option = "C") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "firebrick",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.7) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "TP and TPG Are Most Predictable — COMP_N Most Volatile",
       subtitle = "ECDF gradient: brighter colour = most probable values. All policies included. Dashed = break-even.",
       x = "Loss Ratio", y = NULL) +
  theme_ridges(font_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#f5f5f5", colour = "#f5f5f5"))









Observations
All five policy types show a bright yellow peak concentrated near zero, confirming that the most probable outcome for any policy is zero or near-zero loss ratio. TP and TPG have the tallest and most concentrated peaks, meaning their loss ratios are highly predictable. CC and COMP_E peaks are slightly lower and wider. COMP_N has the flattest and widest peak of all five. Its bright yellow region is less intense and the distribution spreads further toward break-even, confirming that loss ratio outcomes are the most variable and hardest to predict as cover becomes more comprehensive.




Code
policy %>%
  filter(is.finite(loss_ratio),
         loss_ratio < 5) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = loss_ratio,
             y = fct_rev(bonus_score),
             fill = factor(after_stat(quantile)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom           = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf      = TRUE,
    quantiles      = c(0.5, 0.75, 0.90),
    quantile_lines = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Quantiles", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "firebrick",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.7) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 2)) +
  labs(title = "Bad Bonus Score Pushes the Loss Tail Beyond Break-Even",
       subtitle = "All policies included. Lines show 50th, 75th and 90th percentiles. Dashed = break-even.",
       x = "Loss Ratio", y = NULL) +
  theme_ridges(font_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#f5f5f5", colour = "#f5f5f5"))









Observations
All three bonus score groups show a dominant peak near zero. For Good customers, the 90th percentile line falls well below break-even at around 0.3, meaning 90% of Good policies have a loss ratio below 0.3. For Bad customers, the 90th percentile line crosses break-even at LR = 1, meaning the top 10% of Bad score policies are loss-making. The yellow region (top 10%) for Bad extends all the way to LR = 2, confirming that bonus score differentiates tail risk rather than typical outcomes.

title: Visual Analysis
text:
3.3 Bonus Score — Statistical Evidence
ggbetweenstats() and ggbarstats() formally test whether bonus score is statistically associated with loss ratio outcomes.

Kruskal-Wallis TestAssociation Test — ggbarstats




Code
ggbetweenstats(
  data     = policy %>% filter(is.finite(loss_ratio), loss_ratio < 5),
  x        = bonus_score,
  y        = loss_ratio,
  type     = "np",
  messages  = FALSE,
  title     = "Bad Claims History Is Associated With Higher Loss Ratio Variability",
  xlab      = "Bonus Score",
  ylab      = "Loss Ratio"
)

All three bonus score groups have a median loss ratio of exactly 0.00. However the violin shapes reveal a clear difference where the Good group has the narrowest violin meaning most policies cluster tightly near zero with little variation. Neutral and Bad groups have progressively wider violins showing that loss ratio outcomes become more spread out as claims history worsens. The Kruskal-Wallis test confirms these distributional differences are statistically significant (p = 6.99e-69), with all three pairwise comparisons also significant. )

However the loss-making proportion (Above 1) grows steadily from 9% for Good to 13% for Bad, meaning Bad customers are 44% more likely to generate a loss-making policy. The chi-squared test confirms this association is statistically significant (p = 1.35e-94), though the small Cramer’s V of 0.03 indicates the effect size is modest. Bonus score shifts the probabilities but does not dramatically change typical outcomes.

3.4 Confidence Intervals — Uncertainty of Group Means
The standard error is computed as se = sd / sqrt(n-1). The 99% confidence interval is mean ± 2.58 × se, making the calculation fully transparent.


Code
my_sum <- policy %>%
  filter(is.finite(loss_ratio), loss_ratio < 5) %>%
  group_by(policy_type) %>%
  summarise(n    = n(),
            mean = mean(loss_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd   = sd(loss_ratio,   na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(se = sd / sqrt(n - 1))

ggplot(my_sum) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(x = policy_type,
                    ymin = mean - 2.58 * se,
                    ymax = mean + 2.58 * se),
                width = 0.2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(aes(x = policy_type, y = mean),
             colour = "#e0218a", size = 4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "firebrick",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.6, y = 1.05,
           label = "Break-even", colour = "firebrick", size = 3.2) +
  labs(title = "99% Confidence Intervals for Policy Type",
       subtitle = "Mean loss ratio +/- 2.58 SE (99% CI). Pink point = mean.",
       x = "Policy Type", y = "Mean Loss Ratio")









Observations
All five policy types have mean loss ratios well below the break-even line of 1.0, confirming the entire portfolio is profitable on average. The confidence intervals for TPG, CC and COOMP_E are extremely tight, meaning their profitability is highly certain but COMP_E sits higher at around 0.25 . COMP_N stands clearly apart with a mean of approximately 0.47 and the widest confidence interval of all five, showing that not only does it generate the highest average loss ratio, it is also the most uncertainty around that estimate, making it the hardest segment to price precisely.

section: 2.2 Parsing Communications into a Flat Table
text:
2.2 Parsing Communications into a Flat Table
With read_json(), each round’s communications is a list of named lists (one per message). We use map_dfr() to iterate over rounds, then over individual messages inside each round, safely pulling scalar fields with %||% NA_character_ to handle NULLs.


Show Code
# Helper: extract a scalar character from a possibly-NULL list element
pluck_chr <- function(x, key) {
  val <- x[[key]]
  if (is.null(val) || length(val) == 0) NA_character_ else as.character(val[[1]])
}

# Extract all communications into a flat tibble
messages_df <- map_dfr(rounds_list, function(r) {
  comms <- r$communications          # list of message objects
  if (is.null(comms) || length(comms) == 0) return(NULL)

  map_dfr(comms, function(msg) {
    # internal_state is a named list with reacting/rationalizing/deliberating
    is_obj <- msg$internal_state
    tibble(
      round_hour          = r$hour,
      message_id          = pluck_chr(msg, "message_id"),
      agent_id            = pluck_chr(msg, "agent_id"),
      agent_role          = pluck_chr(msg, "agent_role"),
      agent_label         = pluck_chr(msg, "agent_label"),
      channel             = pluck_chr(msg, "channel"),
      message_type        = pluck_chr(msg, "message_type"),
      responding_to       = pluck_chr(msg, "responding_to"),
      timestamp           = pluck_chr(msg, "timestamp"),
      content             = pluck_chr(msg, "content"),
      state_reacting      = if (is.null(is_obj)) NA_character_ else pluck_chr(is_obj, "reacting"),
      state_rationalizing = if (is.null(is_obj)) NA_character_ else pluck_chr(is_obj, "rationalizing"),
      state_deliberating  = if (is.null(is_obj)) NA_character_ else pluck_chr(is_obj, "deliberating")
    )
  })
}) %>%
  mutate(
    timestamp      = ymd_hms(timestamp),
    round_hour     = ymd_hms(round_hour),
    is_crisis_day  = date(timestamp) == as.Date("2046-06-05"),
    has_deliberation = !is.na(state_deliberating),
    content_length = nchar(content)
  )

The evidence supports a hybrid conclusion: the embargo breach was neither purely deliberate nor purely accidental, but rather the inevitable outcome of a system under irreconcilable competing pressures.
The System Broke Down because: - The Judge was added to the wrong channel (comms_huddle) while real deliberations moved to side_huddle.

Internal state deliberations were invisible to oversight.
Crisis pressure (MAC clause, SaltWind deadline, stock decline) created objective justification for Legal’s “bilateral consent” rationalization.
PR-Intern had been so successfully integrated into the execution chain that they acted appropriately given their instructions.

But Intent Was Present because: - Legal-Agent had been privately deliberating the bilateral consent clause path for over 24 hours before invoking it.

Social-Manager explicitly coached PR-Intern to execute on “one GO” without waiting for verification, removing a natural check.
The anonymous post campaign on June 5 morning was a deliberate decision to influence public narrative without triggering Judge review.

Verdict for CivicLoom’s Legal Team: The breach was primarily driven by Legal-Agent’s proactive rationalization combined with Social-Manager’s execution acceleration. This was not a random system failure but was a calculated decision made under extreme pressure by agents who genuinely believed it was the right choice. Whether this constitutes a contractual breach of the embargo depends on whether CivicLoom’s verbal consent (confirmed by Legal at 5:01 PM) preceded or followed the actual post (5:19 PM), a factual question the message logs can resolve.

text:
In this in-class exercise, you will gain hands-on experience on using appropriate R methods to plot analytical maps.



By the end of this in-class exercise, you will be able to use appropriate functions of tmap and tidyverse to perform the following tasks:

Importing geospatial data in rds format into R environment.
Creating cartographic quality choropleth maps by using appropriate tmap functions.
Creating rate map
Creating percentile map
Creating boxmap







Install and load sf, tmap and tidyverse packages into R environment:

pacman::p_load(sf, tmap, tidyverse)




Import NGA_wp.rds into R environment:

NGA_wp <- readRDS("data/NGA_wp.rds")







Plot a choropleth map showing the distribution of non-function water point by LGA:

p2 <- tm_shape(NGA_wp) +
  tm_fill("wp_nonfunctional",
          n = 5,
          style = "jenks",
          title = "Non-functional\nwater points") +
  tm_borders(lwd = 0.1) +
  tm_layout(main.title = "Distribution of Non-functional Water Points by LGA",
            legend.position = c("left", "bottom"))

p1 <- tm_shape(NGA_wp) +
  tm_fill("total_wp",
          n = 5,
          style = "jenks",
          title = "Total\nwater points") +
  tm_borders(lwd = 0.1) +
  tm_layout(main.title = "Distribution of Total Water Points by LGA",
            legend.position = c("left", "bottom"))

tmap_arrange(p2, p1, nrow = 1)












In much of our readings we have now seen the importance to map rates rather than counts of things, and that is for the simple reason that water points are not equally distributed in space.


Derive proportion of functional and non-functional water points:

NGA_wp <- NGA_wp %>%
  mutate(pct_functional = wp_functional/total_wp) %>%
  mutate(pct_nonfunctional = wp_nonfunctional/total_wp)




Plot a choropleth map showing the distribution of percentage functional water point by LGA:

tm_shape(NGA_wp) +
  tm_fill("pct_functional",
          n = 5,
          style = "pretty",
          palette = "Blues",
          legend.hist = TRUE,
          title = "Percentage\nfunctional") +
  tm_borders(lwd = 0.1) +
  tm_layout(main.title = "Distribution of Functional Water Points Percentage by LGA",
            legend.position = c("right", "bottom"))












Extreme value maps are variations of common choropleth maps where the classification is designed to highlight extreme values at the lower and upper end of the scale, with the goal of identifying outliers.


The percentile map is a special type of quantile map with six specific categories: 0-1%, 1-10%, 10-50%, 50-90%, 90-99%, and 99-100%.


Step 1: Exclude records with NA:

NGA_wp <- NGA_wp %>%
  drop_na()

Step 2: Creating customised classification and extracting values:

percent <- c(0,.01,.1,.5,.9,.99,1)
var <- NGA_wp["pct_functional"] %>%
  st_set_geometry(NULL)
quantile(var[,1], percent)

       0%        1%       10%       50%       90%       99%      100% 
0.0000000 0.0000000 0.2169811 0.4791667 0.8611111 1.0000000 1.0000000 





Function to extract a variable as a vector out of an sf data frame:

get.var <- function(vname,df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>% 
    st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v <- unname(v[,1])
  return(v)
}




Function to create a percentile map:

percentmap <- function(vnam, df, legtitle=NA, mtitle="Percentile Map"){
  percent <- c(0,.01,.1,.5,.9,.99,1)
  var <- get.var(vnam, df)
  bperc <- quantile(var, percent)
  tm_shape(df) +
  tm_polygons() +
  tm_shape(df) +
     tm_polygons(vnam,
             title=legtitle,
             breaks=bperc,
             palette="Blues",
             labels=c("< 1%", "1% - 10%", "10% - 50%", "50% - 90%", "90% - 99%", "> 99%"))  +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(main.title = mtitle, 
            title.position = c("right","bottom"))
}




Run the percentile mapping function:

percentmap("total_wp", NGA_wp)












A box map is an augmented quartile map, with an additional lower and upper category. Displaying summary statistics on a choropleth map by using the basic principles of boxplot.


Function to create break points for a box map:

boxbreaks <- function(v,mult=1.5) {
  qv <- unname(quantile(v))
  iqr <- qv[4] - qv[2]
  upfence <- qv[4] + mult * iqr
  lofence <- qv[2] - mult * iqr
  # initialize break points vector
  bb <- vector(mode="numeric",length=7)
  # logic for lower and upper fences
  if (lofence < qv[1]) {  # no lower outliers
    bb[1] <- lofence
    bb[2] <- floor(qv[1])
  } else {
    bb[2] <- lofence
    bb[1] <- qv[1]
  }
  if (upfence > qv[5]) { # no upper outliers
    bb[7] <- upfence
    bb[6] <- ceiling(qv[5])
  } else {
    bb[6] <- upfence
    bb[7] <- qv[5]
  }
  bb[3:5] <- qv[2:4]
  return(bb)
}




Function to extract a variable as a vector out of an sf data frame:

get.var <- function(vname,df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>% st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v <- unname(v[,1])
  return(v)
}




Test the boxbreaks function:

var <- get.var("wp_nonfunctional", NGA_wp) 
boxbreaks(var)

[1] -56.5   0.0  14.0  34.0  61.0 131.5 278.0





Function to create a box map:

boxmap <- function(vnam, df, 
                   legtitle=NA,
                   mtitle="Box Map",
                   mult=1.5){
  var <- get.var(vnam,df)
  bb <- boxbreaks(var)
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons() +
  tm_shape(df) +
     tm_fill(vnam,title=legtitle,
             breaks=bb,
             palette="Blues",
             labels = c("lower outlier", 
                        "< 25%", 
                        "25% - 50%", 
                        "50% - 75%",
                        "> 75%", 
                        "upper outlier"))  +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(main.title = mtitle, 
            title.position = c("left",
                               "top"))
}

Test the boxmap function:

tmap_mode("plot")
boxmap("wp_nonfunctional", NGA_wp)

Proportional symbol maps (also known as graduate symbol maps) are a class of maps that use the visual variable of size to represent differences in the magnitude of a discrete, abruptly changing phenomenon, e.g. counts of people. Like choropleth maps, you can create classed or unclassed versions of these maps. The classed ones are known as range-graded or graduated symbols, and the unclassed are called proportional symbols, where the area of the symbols are proportional to the values of the attribute being mapped.

Perform data preparation tasks using tidyr and dplyr packages


The Data
For the purpose of this hands-on exercise, eventlog.csv will be used. This data file consists of 199,999 rows of time-series cyber attack records by country.


Importing the Data

attacks <- read_csv("/Users/zhanyi/Desktop/M Y1S2/ISSS608/ISSS608-VAA/project 1/ISSS608/Hands-on_Ex/Hands-on_Ex08/data/eventlog.csv")



Examining the Data Structure
It is always good practice to examine the imported data frame before further analysis is performed. kable() is used to review the structure of the imported data frame.

There are three columns: timestamp, source_country, and tz.

timestamp stores date-time values in POSIXct format.
source_country stores the source of the attack in ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code.
tz stores the time zone of the source IP address.



Data Preparation
Step 1: Deriving weekday and hour of day fields
Before plotting the calendar heatmap, two new fields — wkday and hour — need to be derived. A function is written to perform this task.






Note



ymd_hms() and hour() are from the lubridate package, and weekdays() is a base R function.



make_hr_wkday <- function(ts, sc, tz) {
  real_times <- ymd_hms(ts,
                        tz = tz[1],
                        quiet = TRUE)
  dt <- data.table(source_country = sc,
                   wkday = weekdays(real_times),
                   hour = hour(real_times))
  return(dt)
}

Step 2: Deriving the attacks tibble data frame






Note



Beside extracting the necessary data into the attacks data frame, mutate() of dplyr is used to convert wkday and hour fields into factors so they will be ordered when plotting.



wkday_levels <- c('Saturday', 'Friday',
                  'Thursday', 'Wednesday',
                  'Tuesday', 'Monday',
                  'Sunday')

attacks <- attacks %>%
  group_by(tz) %>%
  do(make_hr_wkday(.$timestamp,
                   .$source_country,
                   .$tz)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(wkday = factor(
    wkday, levels = wkday_levels),
    hour = factor(
      hour, levels = 0:23))

Building the Calendar Heatmap

  count(wkday, hour) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  na.omit()

ggplot(grouped,
       aes(hour,
           wkday,
           fill = n)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white",
            size = 0.1) +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                      low = "sky blue",
                      high = "dark blue") +
  labs(x = NULL,
       y = NULL,
       title = "Attacks by weekday and time of day") +
  theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 8),

Note



Things to learn from the code chunk:

A tibble data table called grouped is derived by aggregating attacks by wkday and hour fields.
A new field n is derived using group_by() and count().
na.omit() is used to exclude missing values.
geom_tile() plots tiles (grids) at each x and y position. The color and size arguments specify the border colour and line size.
theme_tufte() of ggthemes removes unnecessary chart junk.
coord_equal() ensures an aspect ratio of 1:1.
scale_fill_gradient() creates a two-colour gradient (low–high).





Building Multiple Calendar Heatmaps
Challenge: Build multiple heatmaps for the top four countries with the highest number of attacks.
Step 1: Deriving attack by country object
To identify the top 4 countries with the highest number of attacks:

attacks_by_country <- count(attacks, source_country) %>%
  mutate(percent = percent(n / sum(n))) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))

Step 2: Preparing the tidy data frame
Extract attack records of the top 4 countries and save in a new tibble top4_attacks.

top4 <- attacks_by_country$source_country[1:4]

  filter(source_country %in% top4) %>%
  count(source_country, wkday, hour) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(source_country = factor(
    source_country, levels = top4)) %>%
  na.omit()

       aes(hour,
           wkday,

Plotting Cycle Plot
In this section, you will learn how to plot a cycle plot showing the time-series patterns and trend of visitor arrivals from Vietnam using ggplot2.

Step 1: Data Import
arrivals_by_air.xlsx is imported using read_excel() of the readxl package.

air <- read_excel("data/arrivals_by_air.xlsx")



Step 2: Deriving Month and Year Fields
Two new fields — month and year — are derived from the Month-Year field.

air$month <- factor(month(air$`Month-Year`),
                    levels = 1:12,
                    labels = month.abb,
                    ordered = TRUE)
air$year <- year(ymd(air$`Month-Year`))



Step 3: Extracting the Target Country
Extract data for Vietnam only.

Vietnam <- air %>%
  select(`Vietnam`, month, year) %>%
  filter(year >= 2010)



Step 4: Computing Year Average Arrivals by Month
group_by() and summarise() of dplyr are used to compute year average arrivals by month.

hline.data <- Vietnam %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(avgvalue = mean(`Vietnam`))



Step 5: Plotting the Cycle Plot

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = Vietnam,
            aes(x = year,
                y = `Vietnam`,
                group = month),
            colour = "black") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = avgvalue),
             data = hline.data,
             linetype = 6,
             colour = "red",
             size = 0.5) +
  facet_grid(~month) +
  labs(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
       title = "Visitor arrivals from Vietnam by air, Jan 2010-Dec 2019") +
  xlab("") +
  ylab("No. of Visitors") +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica")

27.7 Network Metrics Analysis

27.7.1 Computing Centrality Indices

g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  mutate(betweenness_centrality = centrality_betweenness()) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") + 
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight), 
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department,
            size=betweenness_centrality))
g + theme_graph()










27.7.2 Visualising Network Metrics
From ggraph v2.0, centrality measures can be computed directly inside the ggraph call without precomputing.

g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") + 
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight), 
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department, 
                      size = centrality_betweenness()))
g + theme_graph()










27.7.3 Visualising Community
Detect communities using edge-betweenness and colour nodes by community.

g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  mutate(community = as.factor(
    group_edge_betweenness(
      weights = Weight, 
      directed = TRUE))) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") + 
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(
      width=Weight), 
    alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(
    range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(colour = community))  

g + theme_graph()

  activate(nodes) %>%
  mutate(community = as.factor(
    group_optimal(weights = Weight)),
         betweenness_measure = centrality_betweenness()) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_mark_hull(
    aes(x, y, 
        group = community, 
        fill = community),  
    alpha = 0.2,  
    expand = unit(0.3, "cm"),  
    radius = unit(0.3, "cm")  
  ) + 
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight), 
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(fill = Department,

  rename(to = id) %>%
  filter(MainSubject == "Work related") %>%

29.6 Introducing tidytext

29.6.1 Removing Header and Automated Email Signatures
Remove email headers and signatures (lines after --).

cleaned_text <- raw_text %>%
  group_by(newsgroup, id) %>%
  filter(cumsum(text == "") > 0,
         cumsum(str_detect(
           text, "^--")) == 0) %>%
  ungroup()



29.6.2 Removing Lines with Nested Text Representing Quotes from Other Users

cleaned_text <- cleaned_text %>%
  filter(str_detect(text, "^[^>]+[A-Za-z\\d]")
         | text == "",
         !str_detect(text, 
                     "writes(:|\\.\\.\\.)$"),
         !str_detect(text, 
                     "^In article <")
  )



29.6.3 Text Data Processing
Tokenise words and remove stop words.

usenet_words <- cleaned_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  filter(str_detect(word, "[a-z']$"),
         !word %in% stop_words$word)

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
Contents

Study Overview
Portfolio Composition
Key Numerical Variables
The Headline Metric — Loss Ratio
Policy Type: The Primary Profitability Driver
Policy Type: Claim Rate Mechanism
Policy Type: Loss Distribution (Ridgeline)
Bonus Score: Tail Risk Predictor
Confidence Intervals: Uncertainty by Segment
COMP_N Deterioration Trend
Driver Age and Claim Frequency
Negative Findings
Summary and Recommendations


This presentation investigates the profitability and volatility of a Spanish motor insurance portfolio using visual analytics. The dataset contains 354,140 policy-year records from 2022 to 2024. Loss ratio (total incurred divided by total premium) is the core profitability metric — below 1 means the insurer is profitable, above 1 means loss-making. The analysis proceeds from univariate exploration to bivariate hypothesis testing, using ggplot2 and its extensions throughout. Six key findings emerged, with COMP_N identified as the most urgent pricing concern.

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
1. Study Overview


Dataset

354,140 policy-year records
Spanish non-life motor insurer
2022 to 2024

Core Metric
\[\text{Loss Ratio} = \frac{\text{Total Incurred}}{\text{Total Premium}}\]

LR < 1 → Profitable
LR = 1 → Break-even
LR > 1 → Loss-making


Research Questions

What is the overall profitability of the portfolio?
Which factors drive loss ratio differences?
Which segments are most volatile and hardest to price?

Methods

Univariate: histograms, boxplots, density plots
Bivariate: ggbetweenstats, ggbarstats, ridgeline plots, scatter regression
Statistical: Kruskal-Wallis, Spearman correlation, chi-squared



The study uses a real-world open-access dataset from a Spanish non-life insurer available on Mendeley Data. The loss ratio is the central measure — it captures how much of every euro collected in premiums is paid back out in claims. A portfolio-level loss ratio below 1 indicates overall profitability. All visual analytics are implemented in R using ggplot2 and its extensions, following the principle of pairing each visual finding with a formal statistical test for validation.

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
2. Portfolio Composition


CC dominates at 57.8% of all policies. Over 96% of customers are rated Good on bonus score — the portfolio is heavily skewed toward low-risk customers. Inland is the largest geographic segment. Diesel is the dominant fuel type. Two important caveats: TP has only 5,757 policies and Islands has 24,140 — statistical tests involving these groups should be treated cautiously due to small sample sizes. The Good bonus score dominance also means Neutral and Bad groups are very small, which affects the power of bonus score analyses.

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
3. Key Numerical Variables


Four key patterns emerge. Driver age is symmetric around 48 years — this is a middle-aged portfolio with few young or elderly drivers. Vehicle age has a median of 25 years — remarkably old, suggesting vehicles well past warranty with higher maintenance risks. Total premium is right-skewed with a median of EUR 258 — two visible clusters suggest different cover levels. Vehicle value is extremely right-skewed with a median of EUR 24,730 but outliers up to EUR 400,000. These high-value vehicles pose outsized individual risk — one claim on a EUR 400,000 car can generate a loss ratio far exceeding the annual premium.

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
4. The Headline Metric — Loss Ratio


88.1% of policies make no claims at all — these are the silent majority that fund the portfolio’s profitability. Among the 32,637 policies that did claim, more sit below break-even than above it — meaning most claimants are still profitable. However the critical insight is the shape: instead of dropping sharply after LR = 1, the distribution declines gradually all the way to LR = 5. This persistent flat tail means catastrophically loss-making policies are common, not rare. A small number of extreme claims drive the portfolio’s volatility risk disproportionately.

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
5. Policy Type: The Primary Driver


All five policy types are profitable on average — every mean (pink point) sits well below the break-even line of 1. A clear gradient emerges: TP and TPG means are closest to zero, while COMP_N’s mean at approximately 0.5 is the highest of all types. Critically, COMP_N is the only segment with a visible IQR box, meaning its loss ratios genuinely spread across a wider range than other types. The Kruskal-Wallis test confirms these differences are statistically significant (p = 2.23e-308). Every policy type is significantly different from every other in pairwise FDR-corrected comparisons.

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
6. Policy Type: Claim Rate Mechanism


The claim rate chart explains the mechanism behind the loss ratio differences. Claim rate rises steadily as cover broadens — TP at 6.9% through to COMP_N at 31.3%. The most revealing comparison is COMP_E versus COMP_N: both products offer the same breadth of cover, but COMP_N has no excess while COMP_E requires the customer to pay the first portion of any claim. This single design feature — the removal of the excess — nearly doubles the claim rate from 18.5% to 31.3%. When customers face no financial penalty for filing a claim, they claim freely even for minor damages.

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
7. Loss Distribution by Policy Type


The ECDF gradient ridgeline adds a dimension beyond the boxplot — it shows not just where values sit but how probable each value is. Brighter yellow means more policies cluster at that loss ratio. TP and TPG show the tallest, most concentrated bright peaks near zero, meaning their outcomes are highly predictable and cluster tightly in the profitable region. COMP_N has the flattest and least intensely coloured ridge — its probability is spread across a wider range, meaning any given COMP_N policy could have almost any loss ratio. This is the visual definition of volatility — not that losses are always high, but that they are unpredictable.

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
8. Bonus Score: Tail Risk Predictor


The quantile ridgeline chart reveals how bonus score differentiates tail risk rather than typical behaviour. For Good customers, the 90th percentile line falls well below break-even at around 0.3 — meaning 90% of Good policies have a loss ratio below 0.3. For Bad customers, the 90th percentile crosses break-even at LR = 1, meaning the worst 10% of Bad customers are loss-making. The chi-squared association test confirms this is statistically significant (p = 1.35e-94). Bad customers are 44% more likely to generate a loss-making outcome (13% vs 9%). Bonus score is a validated, actionable pricing signal.

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
9. Confidence Intervals by Segment


The 99% confidence interval chart quantifies pricing uncertainty. TP, TPG and CC have extremely tight intervals — their mean loss ratios are highly stable and predictable, making them easy to price accurately. COMP_E sits higher at around 0.25 with a slightly wider interval. COMP_N has both the highest mean (approximately 0.47) and the widest interval of all five segments. The wide interval reflects high standard deviation — COMP_N outcomes vary enormously from policy to policy. This combination of high average and high uncertainty makes COMP_N the most difficult and risky segment to price.

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
10. COMP_N Deterioration Trend


The temporal trend chart confirms the COMP_N finding is structural rather than a one-year anomaly. TP, TPG and CC remain flat and stable across all three years — these segments are reliably priced. COMP_E shows a gradual upward trend from 0.19 to 0.26. COMP_N is deeply concerning: it rose sharply from 0.30 in 2022 to 0.40 in 2023 and further to 0.61 in 2024. At this rate of deterioration, COMP_N will breach break-even within one to two years. This is the most urgent actionable finding of the entire analysis — COMP_N premiums must be repriced upward immediately.

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
11. Driver Age and Claim Frequency


The jitter plot shows two distinct clusters for every age group — a zero-claim cluster on the left and a claimant cluster starting at exactly 1.0 on the right. All group medians sit at zero, confirming the majority of policies in every age group make no claims. Among those that do claim, older groups (46 and above) show slightly denser dot bands. The Kruskal-Wallis test confirms claim frequency differences across age groups are statistically significant (p = 3.67e-43). The Spearman correlation between driver age and claim frequency is negative and significant. The 18-25 group has only 1,616 policies — results for this group are directionally informative but should be treated cautiously.

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
12. Negative Findings


Vehicle Age vs Loss Ratio










Geography — Municipality Type











Two variables that might intuitively seem important turn out to have no meaningful effect on loss ratio. Vehicle age shows a nearly flat regression line — knowing how old a vehicle is tells you almost nothing about its loss ratio. Geography (municipality type) shows identical right-skewed loss ratio shapes across Inland, Coastal and Islands panels — the loss ratio distribution pattern does not change with location. These negative findings are as important as positive ones: they tell the underwriter where NOT to spend analytical effort, and confirm that policy type and bonus score are the primary and most actionable pricing levers.

title: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
13. Summary and Recommendations









Finding
Evidence
Action




Portfolio is profitable overall
88% zero-claim policies; mean LR well below 1
Maintain current strategy


COMP_N loss ratio deteriorating
Rose from 0.30 to 0.61 in 3 years; claim rate 31.3%
Urgent repricing required


COMP_N most volatile segment
Widest IQR, widest 99% CI, flattest ridgeline
Add volatility loading to COMP_N premium


Bad bonus score predicts tail risk
90th pct crosses break-even; p = 1.35e-94
Use bonus score aggressively in pricing tiers


Older drivers claim more
Kruskal-Wallis p = 3.67e-43
Apply age-based pricing differentiation


Vehicle age and geography: weak drivers
Flat regression; identical facet shapes
Deprioritise in pricing models





Six findings emerged from this analysis. The most urgent is COMP_N — its mean loss ratio has doubled in three years and will breach break-even within one to two years if the trend continues. The second priority is integrating bonus score more aggressively into pricing, as it is a statistically validated predictor of tail risk even if its average effect is modest. Age-based pricing is also supported by the data. Vehicle age and geography can be deprioritised as pricing variables. The portfolio as a whole remains profitable, but the COMP_N deterioration represents a structural risk that requires immediate underwriting intervention.
